claim: Dopamine (D2) receptors provide autoinhibitory feedback onto dopamine neurons through interactions with voltage-gated calcium channels and G protein-coupled inwardly-rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels.
source: Dopamine (D2) receptors provide autoinhibitory feedback onto dopamine neurons through well-known interactions with voltage-gated calcium channels and G protein-coupled inwardly-rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on D2 receptor function.

claim: Activation of D2 receptors robustly inhibits isolated sodium leak currents in wild-type mice but not in NALCN conditional knockout mice.
source: We found that activation of D2 receptors robustly inhibits isolated sodium leak currents in wild-type mice but not in NALCN conditional knockout mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing differential effects in wild-type versus knockout mice.

claim: Intracellular GDP-βS abolished the D2 receptor-mediated inhibition of sodium leak current, indicating a G protein-dependent signaling mechanism.
source: Intracellular GDP-βS abolished the inhibition, indicating a G protein-dependent signaling mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using GDP-βS to block G protein signaling.

claim: The application of dopamine reliably slowed pacemaking even when GIRK channels were pharmacologically blocked.
source: The application of dopamine reliably slowed pacemaking even when GIRK channels were pharmacologically blocked.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing dopamine effects in the presence of GIRK channel blockers.

claim: Spontaneous activity was observed in nearly all dopaminergic neurons in wild-type mice, but neurons from NALCN knockouts were mainly silent.
source: Furthermore, while spontaneous activity was observed in nearly all dopaminergic neurons in wild-type mice, neurons from NALCN knockouts were mainly silent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations comparing wild-type and knockout mice.

claim: NALCN is critical for pacemaking in dopaminergic neurons.
source: Both observations demonstrate the critical importance of NALCN for pacemaking in dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations of reduced spontaneous activity in NALCN knockouts.

claim: GABA-B receptor activation produces inhibition of NALCN-mediated currents.
source: Finally, we show that GABA-B receptor activation also produces inhibition of NALCN-mediated currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing GABA-B receptor effects on NALCN currents.

claim: NALCN is a core effector of inhibitory G protein-coupled receptors.
source: Therefore, we identify NALCN as a core effector of inhibitory G protein-coupled receptors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing modulation by both D2 and GABA-B receptors.

claim: D2-receptors are Gi/o protein-coupled receptors that are expressed widely throughout the brain to control a range of behaviors including locomotion, motivation, action selection, and appetitive reward-seeking.
source: Dopamine (D2R) receptors are Gi/o protein-coupled receptors that are expressed widely throughout the brain to control a range of behaviors including locomotion, motivation, action selection, and appetitive reward-seeking (Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Drugs that target D2 receptors have been used for decades as therapies against schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, Huntington's disease and Parkinson's disease.
source: Drugs that target D2 receptors have been used for decades as therapies against schizophrenia, but also for bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, Huntington's disease and Parkinson's disease.
evidence: This claim is based on established medical knowledge about D2 receptor-targeting drugs.

claim: Cocaine increases dopamine levels which then inhibits the activity of dopamine neurons.
source: Drugs of abuse such as cocaine increase dopamine levels which then inhibits the activity of dopamine neurons (Einhorn et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Genetic ablation of D2-autoreceptors leads to hyperactivity and enhanced locomotor responses to cocaine in mice.
source: Genetic ablation of D2-autoreceptors leads to hyperactivity and enhanced locomotor responses to cocaine in mice (Anzalone et al., 2012; Bello et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In midbrain dopamine neurons, somatodendritic D2 receptors autoregulate excitability through inhibition of high-threshold voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: In midbrain dopamine neurons, somatodendritic D2 receptors autoregulate excitability through inhibition of high-threshold voltage-gated calcium channels (Cardozo and Bean, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: D2 receptors couple to GIRK channels to hyperpolarize cells and inhibit tonic firing.
source: In addition, D2 receptors couple to GIRK channels to hyperpolarize cells and inhibit tonic firing (Aghajanian and Bunney, 1977; Beckstead et al., 2004; Lacey et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Genetic ablation of the GIRK2 subunit alone abolishes all GIRK-mediated currents in dopaminergic neurons, resulting in a substantial reduction in both D2 and GABA-B receptor-mediated currents.
source: Genetic ablation of the GIRK2 subunit alone abolishes all GIRK-mediated currents in dopaminergic neurons, resulting in a substantial reduction in both D2 and GABA-B receptor-mediated currents (Beckstead et al., 2004; Cruz et al., 2004; McCall et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A non-GIRK component remains in GIRK2 knockout mice and has yet to be identified.
source: Interestingly, a non-GIRK component remains in GIRK2 knockout mice and has yet to be identified (Cruz et al., 2004; McCall et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Kv1 channels are recruited by D2 receptors to inhibit dopamine release from axon terminals.
source: A potential candidate may be Kv1 channels that are recruited by D2 receptors to inhibit dopamine release from axon terminals (Fulton et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Block of somatodendritic Kv1 channels has little effect on the rate of firing in dopamine cells.
source: However, examination of somatic firing in dopamine cells has shown that block of somatodendritic Kv1 channels has little effect on the rate of firing (Khaliq and Bean, 2008), suggesting that somatic Kv1 channels are unlikely to account for this current.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: NALCN is a non-selective sodium leak channel that is expressed widely in neurons throughout the brain.
source: NALCN is a non-selective sodium leak channel that is expressed widely in neurons throughout the brain (Ren, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mutations in NALCN lead to dysfunction of brainstem respiratory systems in mice.
source: Mutations in NALCN leads to dysfunction of brainstem respiratory systems in mice (Lu et al., 2007; Yeh et al., 2017), disrupted circadian rhythms in flies (Flourakis et al., 2015), motor dysfunction in C. elegans (Gao et al., 2015), and cognitive defects in humans (Bend et al., 2016; Chong et al., 2015; Lozic et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations in NALCN lead to disrupted circadian rhythms in flies.
source: Mutations in NALCN leads to dysfunction of brainstem respiratory systems in mice (Lu et al., 2007; Yeh et al., 2017), disrupted circadian rhythms in flies (Flourakis et al., 2015), motor dysfunction in C. elegans (Gao et al., 2015), and cognitive defects in humans (Bend et al., 2016; Chong et al., 2015; Lozic et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations in NALCN lead to motor dysfunction in C. elegans.
source: Mutations in NALCN leads to dysfunction of brainstem respiratory systems in mice (Lu et al., 2007; Yeh et al., 2017), disrupted circadian rhythms in flies (Flourakis et al., 2015), motor dysfunction in C. elegans (Gao et al., 2015), and cognitive defects in humans (Bend et al., 2016; Chong et al., 2015; Lozic et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations in NALCN lead to cognitive defects in humans.
source: Mutations in NALCN leads to dysfunction of brainstem respiratory systems in mice (Lu et al., 2007; Yeh et al., 2017), disrupted circadian rhythms in flies (Flourakis et al., 2015), motor dysfunction in C. elegans (Gao et al., 2015), and cognitive defects in humans (Bend et al., 2016; Chong et al., 2015; Lozic et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NALCN-mediated currents depolarize the resting membrane potential in hippocampal neurons.
source: At the cellular level, NALCN-mediated currents depolarize the resting membrane potential in hippocampal neurons (Lu et al., 2007) and drive spontaneous firing in GABAergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars reticulata (Lutas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NALCN-mediated currents drive spontaneous firing in GABAergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars reticulata.
source: At the cellular level, NALCN-mediated currents depolarize the resting membrane potential in hippocampal neurons (Lu et al., 2007) and drive spontaneous firing in GABAergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars reticulata (Lutas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NALCN channels are activated by tachykinin- and neurotensin-receptors through a G protein-independent, tyrosine kinase-dependent mechanism.
source: In addition to generating a sodium leak current, NALCN channels are activated by tachykinin- and neurotensin-receptors through a G protein-independent, tyrosine kinase-dependent mechanism (Lu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The calcium sensor receptor (CaSR) regulates NALCN in a G-protein dependent manner.
source: By contrast, the calcium sensor receptor (CaSR) regulates NALCN in a G-protein dependent manner (Lu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Behavioral experiments in C. elegans suggest that the nematode dopamine receptor, Dop-3, modulates ortholog Na+ leak channels, NCA-1 and NCA-2.
source: Interestingly, behavioral experiments in C. elegans suggest that the nematode dopamine receptor, Dop-3, modulates ortholog Na+ leak channels, NCA-1 and NCA-2 (Topalidou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Direct electrophysiological evidence for modulation of NALCN by dopamine receptors in mammalian neurons is lacking.
source: However, direct electrophysiological evidence for modulation is lacking and results may differ in mammalian neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior evidence in the literature.

claim: Sodium replacement with NMDG resulted in a reduction of the average holding current from −40.7 ± 10.18 to −13.75 ± 7.39 pA (n = 8; p = 0.0078).
source: As shown in Figure 1B,C, sodium replacement with NMDG resulted in a reduction of the average holding current (Vhold = −70 mV) from −40.7 ± 10.18 to −13.75 ± 7.39 pA (n = 8; p = 0.0078, Wilcoxon).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Lowering extracellular calcium from 2 mM to 0.1 mM increased the resting sodium leak current from −50.69 ± 5.35 pA to −192 ± 20.07 pA (n = 22, p < 0.0001).
source: Switching to low calcium solution, the resting sodium leak current increased dramatically over a time-course of 6–10 min from an amplitude of −50.69 ± 5.35 pA to −192 ± 20.07 pA (n = 22, Figure 1D–F; p < 0.0001, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Blocking the resting sodium leak conductance with NMDG substitution reduced the holding current from −192 ± 20.07 pA to −64.53 ± 8.96 pA (n = 22; p < 0.0001).
source: Blocking the resting sodium leak conductance with NMDG substitution reduced the holding current from −192 ± 20.07 pA to −64.53 ± 8.96 pA (n = 22; Figure 1D–F; p < 0.0001, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: In NALCN conditional knockout mice, lowering extracellular calcium resulted in only a slight increase in Na+ leak current from −20.83 ± 2.279 to −34.76 ± 3.659 pA (n = 9; p = 0.03).
source: In knockout cells, there was relatively little effect of lowering extracellular calcium. Instead, we observed only a slight increase in Na+ leak current from −20.83 ± 2.279 to −34.76 ± 3.659 pA (n = 9; p = 0.03, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from NALCN knockout mice.

claim: In NALCN conditional knockout mice, subsequent substitution of sodium with NMDG solution did not significantly reduce the holding current (normal Na+, −34.76 ± 3.659 pA; NMDG, −24.58 ± 4.72 pA; n = 9, p = 0.14).
source: Moreover, subsequent substitution of sodium with NMDG solution did not significantly reduce the holding current (normal Na+, −34.76 ± 3.659 pA; NMDG, −24.58 ± 4.72 pA; n = 9, p = 0.14, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: The low calcium potentiation of the sodium leak reflects potentiation of current flowing through NALCN channels.
source: Therefore, in agreement with the work of Ren and colleagues in hippocampal neurons (Lu et al., 2010), our experiments in dopaminergic neurons demonstrate that the low calcium potentiation of the sodium leak reflects potentiation of current flowing through NALCN channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with prior research.

claim: Bath application of dopamine led to inhibition of the leak current from −201.1 ± 19.03 pA under control conditions to −133.9 ± 14.68 pA at the time of maximal dopamine inhibition (n = 14; p < 0.0001).
source: Bath application of dopamine led to inhibition of the leak current from −201.1 ± 19.03 pA under control conditions to −133.9 ± 14.68 pA at the time of maximal dopamine inhibition (n = 14; p < 0.0001, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) (Figure 2A,G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,G,H.

claim: 88.08 ± 8.36% of the total sodium leak was inhibited by dopamine.
source: We found that 88.08 ± 8.36% of the total sodium leak was inhibited by dopamine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: The dopamine inhibition of the sodium leak was completely abolished in the NALCN conditional knockout mouse (low Ca2+, −57.94 ± 11.62 pA; dopamine, −65.31 ± 19 pA; n = 7; p = 0.185).
source: The dopamine inhibition of the sodium leak was completely abolished in the NALCN conditional knockout mouse (low Ca2+, −57.94 ± 11.62 pA; dopamine, −65.31 ± 19 pA; n = 7; p = 0.185, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) (Figure 2B,G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,G,H.

claim: The concentration of half-maximal inhibition (IC50) of NALCN by dopamine was 725 nM (range, 491–961 nM; Hill coefficient, −0.6; range, 0.4–0.7).
source: Examination of the concentration-response curve in Figure 2C shows that the concentration of half-maximal inhibition (IC50) of NALCN by dopamine was 725 nM (range, 491–961 nM; Hill coefficient, −0.6; range, 0.4–0.7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The IC50 value for dopamine inhibition of NALCN is comparable to the published EC50 values of 155 nM and 233 nM for dopamine activation of GIRK channels.
source: This value is comparable to the published EC50 values of 155 nM and 233 nM for dopamine activation of GIRK channels (Kim et al., 1995; Uchida et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited literature values.

claim: Dopamine inhibition of NALCN was still present in Arr2 knockout mice with a reduction of the sodium leak current from −179.3 ± 18.72 to −122.5 ± 12.82 pA (n = 6; p = 0.012).
source: We found that dopamine inhibition of NALCN was still present in Arr2 knockout mice with a reduction of the sodium leak current from −179.3 ± 18.72 to −122.5 ± 12.82 pA (n = 6; p = 0.012, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from β-arrestin2 knockout mice.

claim: There was no difference in the amplitude of the dopamine-sensitive sodium leak current between wild-type (67.24 ± 8.96 pA; n = 14) and Arr2 knockouts (56.86 ± 10.75 pA; n = 6) (p = 0.866).
source: Comparing the amplitude of the dopamine-sensitive sodium leak current, we observed no difference between wild-type (67.24 ± 8.96 pA; n = 14) and Arr2 knockouts (56.86 ± 10.75 pA; n = 6) (p = 0.866, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: Substitution of GTP with GDP-βS in the intracellular solution completely abolished the D2 receptor-mediated inhibition of the NALCN current.
source: Substitution of GTP with GDP-βS in the intracellular solution completely abolished the D2 receptor-mediated inhibition of the NALCN current.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using GDP-βS.

claim: Internal GDP-βS blocked the effect of dopamine when recordings were made in external solution containing 2 mM Ca2+ (control, −125.9 ± 20.73 pA; dopamine, −131.2 ± 19.9 pA; n = 8; p = 0.4196).
source: Internal GDP-βS blocked the effect of dopamine when recordings were made in external solution containing 2 mM Ca2+ (control, −125.9 ± 20.73 pA; dopamine, −131.2 ± 19.9 pA; n = 8; p = 0.4196, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Internal GDP-βS blocked the effect of dopamine when recordings were made in 0.1 mM external Ca2+ solution (control, −196.4 ± 12.07 pA; dopamine, −195.0 ± 14.72 pA; n = 5; p = 0.9992).
source: Similar results were obtained in recordings made in 0.1 mM external Ca2+ solution (control, −196.4 ± 12.07 pA; dopamine, −195.0 ± 14.72 pA; n = 5; p = 0.9992, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: D2 receptors inhibit NALCN in a G protein-dependent manner.
source: All together, these results demonstrate that D2 receptors inhibit NALCN in a G protein-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the GDP-βS experiments.

claim: In wild-type animals, 135 out of 148 of dopaminergic neurons (91.21%, 33 mice) were spontaneously active with firing frequencies above 0.1 Hz.
source: In wild-type animals, we found that 135 out of 148 of dopaminergic neurons (91.21%, 33 mice) were spontaneously active with firing frequencies above 0.1 Hz.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in wild-type mice.

claim: In NALCN conditional knockout mice, only 18 out of 60 (30%, 18 mice) dopamine neurons were spontaneously active.
source: In NALCN conditional knockout mice, however, we were surprised to find that only a minor fraction of dopamine neurons, 18 out of 60 (30%, 18 mice) were spontaneously active (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In silent dopaminergic neurons from NALCN knockout mice, the resting membrane potential immediately following breakthrough was hyperpolarized at an average of −53.65 ± 0.71 mV (n = 15).
source: In these silent dopaminergic neurons, the resting membrane potential immediately following breakthrough was hyperpolarized at an average of −53.65 ± 0.71 mV (n = 15).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Small current injections of 10–20 pA in silent NALCN knockout neurons was sufficient to restore a regular tonic firing activity at 0.5 to 5 Hz.
source: However, small current injections of 10–20 pA in these cells was sufficient to restore a regular tonic firing activity at 0.5 to 5 Hz (Figure 3B), indicating that these cells were healthy and capable of firing action potentials.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NALCN currents play a central role in generating the depolarization necessary for driving pacemaking in dopaminergic neurons.
source: These data show that although NALCN currents are small in amplitude when recorded in physiological external calcium, they play a central role in generating the depolarization necessary for driving pacemaking in dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations of reduced spontaneous activity in NALCN knockouts.

claim: In the presence of GIRK channel blockers, dopamine application resulted in a substantial reduction in firing from 2.56 ± 0.18 to 0.89 ± 0.26 Hz (n = 8; p = 0.0078).
source: In the presence of GIRK channel blockers, dopamine application resulted in a substantial reduction in firing from 2.56 ± 0.18 to 0.89 ± 0.26 Hz (n = 8; p = 0.0078, Wilcoxon test) (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Dopamine reduced firing in wild-type mice even in the presence of GIRK channel blockers from 3.71 ± 0.32 to 1.71 ± 0.32 Hz (n = 9; p = 0.0039) in whole-cell configuration.
source: Similar to our cell-attached recordings, dopamine reduced firing in wild-type mice even in the presence of GIRK channel blockers 3.71 ± 0.32 to 1.71 ± 0.32 Hz (n = 9; p = 0.0039, Wilcoxon test) (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Dopamine neurons recorded in the NALCN conditional knockout showed no reduction in firing when dopamine was applied in the presence of BaCl2 and tertiapin-Q (NALCN cKO mice; control, 3.024 ± 0.22 Hz; dopamine, 3.31 ± 0.25 Hz; n = 8; p = 0.078).
source: By contrast, dopamine neurons recorded in the NALCN conditional knockout showed no reduction in firing when dopamine was applied in the presence of BaCl2 and tertiapin-Q. In fact, we observed a trend toward a small increase in the firing rate following puff application of dopamine (NALCN cKO mice; control, 3.024 ± 0.22 Hz; dopamine, 3.31 ± 0.25 Hz; n = 8; p = 0.078, Wilcoxon test) (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: NALCN channels contribute significantly to pacemaking in dopamine neurons.
source: Therefore, these results demonstrate that NALCN channels contribute significantly to pacemaking in dopamine neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Even under conditions where GIRK currents are blocked, spontaneous firing is slowed by dopamine inhibition of NALCN channels alone.
source: Moreover, we show that even under conditions where GIRK currents are blocked, spontaneous firing is slowed by dopamine inhibition of NALCN channels alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing dopamine effects in the presence of GIRK blockers.

claim: Bath application of baclofen 10 µM reduced the holding current from −185 ± 16.06 pA to −106 ± 13.89 pA in baclofen (n = 8; p = 0.0041).
source: Recording the isolated sodium leak current at −70 mV in low calcium, we found that bath application of baclofen 10 µM reduced the holding current from −185 ± 16.06 pA to −106 ± 13.89 pA in baclofen (n = 8; p = 0.0041, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The baclofen-sensitive current was similar in amplitude to the dopamine-sensitive current (baclofen-sensitive current, 79 ± 14.13 pA, n = 8; dopamine-sensitive current, 67.24 ± 8.96 pA, n = 14; p = 0.66).
source: Furthermore, the baclofen-sensitive current was similar in amplitude to the dopamine-sensitive current (baclofen-sensitive current, 79 ± 14.13 pA, n = 8; dopamine-sensitive current, 67.24 ± 8.96 pA, n = 14; p = 0.66, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: Following baclofen application, substitution of sodium with NMDG produced no further block of the sodium leak currents (p = 0.21).
source: We found that following baclofen application, substitution of sodium with NMDG produced no further block of the sodium leak currents (p = 0.21, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) indicating that activation of GABA-B receptors results in nearly complete inhibition of sodium leak currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Activation of GABA-B receptors results in nearly complete inhibition of sodium leak currents.
source: We found that following baclofen application, substitution of sodium with NMDG produced no further block of the sodium leak currents (p = 0.21, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) indicating that activation of GABA-B receptors results in nearly complete inhibition of sodium leak currents.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observation that NMDG produced no further block after baclofen.

claim: The baclofen inhibition of the isolated sodium leak current recorded at −70 mV was completely abolished in cells from NALCN conditional knockout mice (low Ca2+, −54.47 ± 13.57 pA; baclofen, −61.89 ± 12.52 pA, n = 7, p = 0.0436).
source: Similar to our results examining dopamine, the baclofen inhibition of the isolated sodium leak current recorded at −70 mV was completely abolished in cells from NALCN conditional knockout mice (low Ca2+, −54.47 ± 13.57 pA; baclofen, −61.89 ± 12.52 pA, n = 7, p = 0.0436, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) (Figure 4B), demonstrating that GABA-B receptors inhibit sodium leak currents flowing through NALCN channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GABA-B receptors inhibit sodium leak currents flowing through NALCN channels.
source: Similar to our results examining dopamine, the baclofen inhibition of the isolated sodium leak current recorded at −70 mV was completely abolished in cells from NALCN conditional knockout mice (low Ca2+, −54.47 ± 13.57 pA; baclofen, −61.89 ± 12.52 pA, n = 7, p = 0.0436, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) (Figure 4B), demonstrating that GABA-B receptors inhibit sodium leak currents flowing through NALCN channels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data in NALCN knockout mice.

claim: In the presence of BaCl2 and tertiapin-Q, a significant decrease of the firing was induced by the baclofen puff in wild-type (from 3.67 ± 0.29 to 0.76 ± 0.37 Hz; n = 8, p = 0.0002).
source: In the presence of BaCl2 and tertiapin-Q, a significant decrease of the firing was induced by the baclofen puff in wild-type (from 3.67 ± 0.29 to 0.76 ± 0.37 Hz; n = 8, p = 0.0002, Wilcoxon) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: BaCl2 and tertiapin-Q completely abolished the effect of baclofen on firing in dopamine neurons recorded in NALCN conditional knockout mice (frequency, control, 3.02 ± 0.71 Hz; baclofen, 3.02 ± 0.66 Hz; n = 8; p > 0.99).
source: By contrast, BaCl2 and tertiapin-Q completely abolished the effect of baclofen on firing in dopamine neurons recorded in NALCN conditional knockout mice (frequency, control, 3.02 ± 0.71 Hz; baclofen, 3.02 ± 0.66 Hz; n = 8; p > 0.99, Wilcoxon) (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Past studies have reported EC50 values of 9.2 µM and 14.8 µM for baclofen activation of GIRK channels.
source: Past studies have tested the sensitivity of GIRK channels to baclofen and have reported EC50 values of 9.2 µM and 14.8 µM (Chan et al., 1998; Cruz et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 10 µM baclofen produced a near complete inhibition of sodium leak current.
source: By contrast, our experiments above show that 10 µM baclofen produced a near complete inhibition of sodium leak current (Figure 4A), suggesting a much higher potency of baclofen in the modulation of NALCN channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The IC50 value for baclofen inhibition of NALCN is 267 nM (range, 234–301 nM; Hill coefficient, −1.1; range, 0.9–1.3).
source: Concentration-dependence curves yielded an IC50 value for baclofen of 267 nM (range, 234–301 nM; Hill coefficient, −1.1; range, 0.9–1.3), more than an order of magnitude lower than the published EC50 value for baclofen activation of GIRK.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from concentration-response curves.

claim: The IC50 for baclofen inhibition of NALCN is more than an order of magnitude lower than the published EC50 value for baclofen activation of GIRK.
source: Concentration-dependence curves yielded an IC50 value for baclofen of 267 nM (range, 234–301 nM; Hill coefficient, −1.1; range, 0.9–1.3), more than an order of magnitude lower than the published EC50 value for baclofen activation of GIRK.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with published values.

claim: Baclofen delivered at 300 nM reduced the firing frequency of dopamine neurons by 44.79%, from 2.39 ± 0.41 Hz to 1.07 ± 0.28 Hz (n = 7, p = 0.0039).
source: Baclofen delivered at 300 nM reduced the firing frequency of dopamine neurons by 44.79%, from 2.39 ± 0.41 Hz to 1.07 ± 0.28 Hz (n = 7, p = 0.0039, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Baclofen delivered at concentrations that are below the range necessary to activate GIRK channels can significantly inhibit excitability, primarily through inhibition of NALCN.
source: Therefore, these results demonstrate that baclofen delivered at concentrations that are below the range necessary to activate GIRK channels can significantly inhibit excitability, primarily through inhibition of NALCN.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations with 300 nM baclofen.

claim: NALCN is a major ionic contributor to the generation of spontaneous activity in midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
source: These data demonstrate that NALCN is a major ionic contributor to the generation of spontaneous activity in midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: The NALCN-mediated sodium leak conductance is negatively modulated by both dopamine D2 receptors and GABA-B receptors.
source: Furthermore, we provide the first evidence that the NALCN-mediated sodium leak conductance is negatively modulated by both dopamine D2 receptors and GABA-B receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing inhibition by both receptor types.

claim: Modulation of NALCN leads to significant slowing of spontaneous activity.
source: We also show that modulation of NALCN leads to significant slowing of spontaneous activity, consistent with its role in driving pacemaking.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on firing rate changes.

claim: Baclofen exhibits a higher potency in inhibiting NALCN than for activating GIRK channels.
source: Lastly, we show that baclofen exhibits a higher potency in inhibiting NALCN than for activating GIRK channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of IC50 and EC50 values.

claim: NALCN is a core effector of Gi/o protein-coupled receptors that functions in concert with GIRK channels to inhibit neuronal firing in midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
source: Thus, we identify the NALCN channel as a core effector of Gi/o protein-coupled receptors that functions in concert with GIRK channels to inhibit neuronal firing in midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: Voltage-clamp experiments using ion substitution have identified prominent subthreshold sodium leak currents in dopamine neurons.
source: Voltage-clamp experiments using ion substitution have identified prominent subthreshold sodium leak currents in dopamine neurons (Khaliq and Bean, 2010), GABAergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) (Atherton and Bevan, 2005), neurons of the cerebellar nucleus (Raman et al., 2000) and suprachiasmatic nucleus neurons (Jackson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Knockout of NALCN in SNr GABAergic neurons and chemosensory neurons of the retrotrapezoid nucleus results in hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential and a ~ 50% reduction in spontaneous firing rate.
source: Consistent with these findings, recent studies in SNr GABAergic neurons and chemosensory neurons of the retrotrapezoid nucleus have found that knockout of NALCN results in hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential and a ~ 50% reduction in spontaneous firing rate (Lutas et al., 2016; Yeh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In circadian pacemaker neurons, knockout of NALCN leads to nearly complete abolishment of pacemaking.
source: In circadian pacemaker neurons, knockout of NALCN leads to nearly complete abolishment of pacemaking (Flourakis et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Background sodium leak currents in VTA dopamine neurons are large in amplitude, while sodium leak currents in SNc neurons are relatively small.
source: A previous study of the conductances that drive pacemaking reported that background sodium leak currents in VTA dopamine neurons are large in amplitude, while sodium leak currents in SNc neurons are relatively small (Khaliq and Bean, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Heterogeneity may exist across subpopulations of SNc neurons either in NALCN expression and/or differences in the regulation of NALCN by external calcium through the calcium sensing receptor (CaSR).
source: In addition to the previously described differences in leak currents between VTA and SNc neurons (Khaliq and Bean, 2010), however, heterogeneity may also exist across subpopulations of SNc neurons either in NALCN expression and/or differences in the regulation of NALCN by external calcium through the calcium sensing receptor (CaSR).
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting possible explanations for observed differences.

claim: Action potential firing is generated by multiple subthreshold conductances with overlapping functions, an arrangement that favors compensatory adaptation when single conductances are inhibited.
source: Action potential firing is generate by multiple subthreshold conductances with overlapping functions, an arrangement that favors compensatory adaptation when single conductances are inhibited (Drion et al., 2011; Guzman et al., 2010; Kimm et al., 2015; Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Swensen and Bean, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Knockout of CaV1.3 L-type calcium channels has little effect on firing in dopamine neurons due to upregulation of T-type channels.
source: As an example, CaV1.3 L-type calcium channels are active during pacemaking in dopamine neurons, but knockout of CaV1.3 has little effect on firing (Blythe et al., 2009) due to upregulation of T-type channels (Poetschke et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Homeostatic compensation in NALCN knockout mice may have occurred at the level of synaptic drive onto the dopamine neurons.
source: Alternatively, compensation may have occurred at the level of synaptic drive onto the dopamine neurons.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting a possible explanation.

claim: GABA-B receptors in hippocampus and entorhinal cortex have been shown to activate background leak tandem-pore potassium (K2P) channels, TREK1 and 2.
source: For example, GABA-B receptors in hippocampus and entorhinal cortex have been shown to activate background leak tandem-pore potassium (K2P) channels, TREK1 and 2 (Breton and Stuart, 2017; Deng et al., 2009; Sandoz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In VTA dopamine neurons recorded in GIRK2 knockouts, activation of GABA-B receptors evokes a Ba2+ insensitive, non-GIRK current that was hypothesized to be produced by K2P channels.
source: In VTA dopamine neurons recorded in GIRK2 knockouts, activation of GABA-B receptors evokes a Ba2+ insensitive, non-GIRK current that was hypothesized to be produced by K2P channels (Cruz et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Differences may exist between GABA-B signaling in SNc and VTA dopamine neurons.
source: These observations suggest that differences may exist between GABA-B signaling in SNc and VTA dopamine neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations in this study compared to prior research.

claim: GIRK channels exhibit EC50 values for baclofen in the range of 0.9–4.5 μM in midbrain GABAergic neurons and hippocampal neurons.
source: By comparison, GIRK channels exhibit a much lower sensitivity to baclofen according to published EC50 values in dopamine neurons (9.2 and 14.8 μM) (Chan et al., 1998; Cruz et al., 2004) and in other neurons such as midbrain GABAergic neurons and hippocampal neurons (range, 0.9–4.5 μM) (Chan et al., 1998; Cruz et al., 2004; Sodickson and Bean, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The proximity of GABA-B receptor to inhibitory synapses may determine the extent to which NALCN or GIRK channels are recruited.
source: However, one possibility is that the proximity of GABA-B receptor to inhibitory synapses may determine the extent to which NALCN or GIRK channels are recruited.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting a possible mechanism.

claim: GABA-B receptors located close to synapses are exposed to high GABA concentrations which would favor GIRK activation.
source: GABA-B receptors located close to synapses are exposed to high GABA concentrations which would favor GIRK activation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on logical inference about receptor location and GABA concentration.

claim: Modulation through extrasynaptic GABA-B receptors, which are activated by lower concentrations of GABA, may primarily involve inhibition of NALCN.
source: On the other hand, modulation through extrasynaptic GABA-B receptors, which are activated by lower concentrations of GABA, may primarily involve inhibition of NALCN.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting a possible mechanism based on receptor location.

claim: Activation of GIRK channels decreases input resistance while inhibition of NALCN increases input resistance.
source: While both hyperpolarize the membrane potential, activation of GIRK channels decreases input resistance while inhibition of NALCN increases input resistance.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the effects of these channels on membrane properties.

claim: Simultaneous inhibition of NALCN may function to potentiate GIRK-mediated hyperpolarization.
source: As a result, simultaneous inhibition of NALCN may function to potentiate GIRK-mediated hyperpolarization.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting a possible functional interaction.

claim: NALCN currents are inhibited nearly maximally by activation of either GABA-B and D2 receptors.
source: Indeed, we find that NALCN currents are inhibited nearly maximally by activation of either GABA-B and D2 receptors (see Figures 2A and 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 4A.

claim: GABA-B and D2 receptors may be arranged spatially into overlapping microdomains in which both receptors have access to GIRK channels and the NALCN signaling complex.
source: This suggests an interesting scenario where GABA-B and D2 receptors may be arranged spatially into overlapping microdomains in which both receptors have access to GIRK channels and the NALCN signaling complex.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting a possible spatial arrangement.

claim: GIRK channels are inhibited by intracellular calcium but enhanced by internal sodium ions.
source: Likewise, it has been shown that GIRK channels are inhibited by intracellular calcium but enhanced by internal sodium ions (Kramer and Williams, 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: VTA dopamine neurons that project to medial and lateral nucleus accumbens differ markedly in their responses to baclofen.
source: Specifically, VTA dopamine neurons that project to medial and lateral nucleus accumbens differ markedly in their responses to baclofen (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The expression level of GIRK2 mRNA is 10 times lower in dopaminergic neurons of the medial VTA relative to laterally located mesostriatal dopamine neurons.
source: In addition, past work has shown that the expression level of GIRK2 mRNA is 10 times lower in dopaminergic neurons of the medial VTA relative to laterally located mesostriatal dopamine neurons (Lammel et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Bath application of both GABA and baclofen silenced the firing of mesocortical dopamine neurons completely despite low GIRK expression.
source: Interestingly, despite the low expression of GIRK expression in mesocortical cells, it was shown that bath application of both GABA and baclofen silenced the firing of mesocortical dopamine neurons completely.
evidence: This claim is based on prior research findings.

claim: Inhibition of NALCN channels alone is sufficient to slow down the firing rate.
source: Our data demonstrate that inhibition of NALCN channels alone is sufficient to slow down the firing rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study.

claim: Both GABA-B and D2 receptors modulate NALCN, raising the possibility that this may be a common feature to other Gi/o protein-coupled receptors across different neuronal cell types.
source: Collectively, our findings provide evidence that NALCN is an effector of Gi/o coupled receptors in dopamine neurons. Both GABA-B and D2 receptors modulate NALCN, raising the possibility that this may be a common feature to other Gi/o protein-coupled receptors across different neuronal cell types.
evidence: This claim is speculative, extrapolating from the experimental findings.

claim: Mice were generated in which positions between exons 5 and 6 of the NALCN allele was flanked by lox-P sites (Nalcnflox).
source: We generated mice in which positions between exons 5 and 6 of the NALCN allele was flanked by lox-P sites (Nalcnflox).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used to generate the knockout mice.

claim: Nalcnflox mice were bred to Slc6a3-Cre mice, resulting in offspring (Nalcnflox/flox; Slc6a3Cre) that lack expression of NALCN in dopaminergic neurons.
source: Nalcnflox mice were then bred to Slc6a3-Cre mice, resulting in offspring (Nalcnflox/flox; Slc6a3Cre) that lack expression of NALCN in dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used to generate the conditional knockout mice.

claim: A recent publication reported Nalcnflox mice that were generated independently using ES cells obtained from the same source (KOMP), with exon deletion sites that are exactly the same as those reported in this study.
source: A recent publication reported Nalcnflox mice that were generated independently using ES cells obtained from the same source (KOMP), with exon deletion sites that are exactly the same as those reported in this study (Yeh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cs+-based intracellular recording solution (CsMeSO3) was used to block potassium conductances.
source: To determine the contribution of NALCN to background leak currents in dopamine neurons in coronal brain slices from adult mice, we first isolated sodium leak currents using a Cs+-based intracellular recording solution (CsMeSO3) to block potassium conductances.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Tetrodotoxin (1 µM), CsCl (3 mM), and apamin (300 nM) were included in the extracellular solution to block voltage-gated sodium channels, hyperpolarization-gated (Ih) channels and small-conductance calcium-activated (SK) channels.
source: In addition, tetrodotoxin (1 µM), CsCl (3 mM), and apamin (300 nM) were included in the extracellular solution to block voltage-gated sodium channels, hyperpolarization-gated (Ih) channels and small-conductance calcium-activated (SK) channels (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used.

claim: There was no difference in the amplitude of NMDG-sensitive currents when recording with either Cs+-based or K+-based internal solutions (NMDG-sensitive current at −70 mV; Cs+-based, 138 ± 18 pA, n = 22; K+-based, 107.9 ± 17 pA, n = 8; p = 0.36).
source: We observed no difference in the amplitude of NMDG-sensitive currents when recording with either Cs+-based or K+-based internal solutions (NMDG-sensitive current at −70 mV; Cs+-based, 138 ± 18 pA, n = 22; K+-based, 107.9 ± 17 pA, n = 8; p = 0.36).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different recording conditions.

claim: GIRK channels are not Cs+ permeable.
source: GIRK channels are not Cs+ permeable, suggesting that our Cs+-based internal solution is sufficient to block most of GIRK currents (Watts et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 100 µM BaCl2 was added to the bath solution to ensure that GIRK channels were blocked.
source: To ensure that GIRK channels were blocked in this set of experiments, we added 100 µM BaCl2 to the bath solution.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Subsequent NMDG substitution did not further reduce holding current after dopamine application (dopamine, −133.9 ± 14.68 pA;NMDG, −116.2 ± 13.31 pA, n = 14; p = 0.43).
source: Subsequent NMDG substitution did not further reduce holding current (dopamine, −133.9 ± 14.68 pA;NMDG, −116.2 ± 13.31 pA, n = 14; p = 0.43, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) (Figure 2A and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and G.

claim: Cells that were recorded using GDP-βS internal solution showed a slow but steady increase in the inward leak current (1–2 min after breakthrough, −67.69 ± 12.75 pA;~15 min following breakthrough, −125.9 ± 20.73 pA; n = 8; p = 0.0027).
source: Upon breakthrough, cells that were recorded using GDP-βS internal solution showed a slow but steady increase in the inward leak current (1–2 min after breakthrough, −67.69 ± 12.75 pA;~15 min following breakthrough, −125.9 ± 20.73 pA; n = 8; p = 0.0027, RM one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey test) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The enhancement in leak current with GDP-βS is likely due to GDP-βS dependent disruption in signaling from calcium sensing (CaSR) receptors, which produce an incomplete but constitutive inhibition of NALCN-mediated leak currents in the presence of extracellular calcium.
source: The enhancement in leak current is likely due to GDP-βS dependent disruption in signaling from calcium sensing (CaSR) receptors, which produce an incomplete but constitutive inhibition of NALCN-mediated leak currents in the presence of extracellular calcium (Lu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations and supported by a citation.

claim: The isolated sodium leak current holding current at −70 mV in wild-type mice was −55.74 ± 4.29 pA (n = 39).
source: The small amplitude of the sodium leak currents recorded in 2 mM external calcium raises the question of whether inhibition of NALCN by dopamine would have a significant physiological effect on firing in the absence of GIRK activation (holding current at −70 mV; wild-type, −55.74 ± 4.29 pA, n = 39; NALCN KO, −19.69 ± 3.72 pA, n = 20; p < 0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The isolated sodium leak current holding current at −70 mV in NALCN KO mice was −19.69 ± 3.72 pA (n = 20).
source: The small amplitude of the sodium leak currents recorded in 2 mM external calcium raises the question of whether inhibition of NALCN by dopamine would have a significant physiological effect on firing in the absence of GIRK activation (holding current at −70 mV; wild-type, −55.74 ± 4.29 pA, n = 39; NALCN KO, −19.69 ± 3.72 pA, n = 20; p < 0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The difference in holding current at −70 mV between wild-type and NALCN KO mice was statistically significant (p < 0.0001).
source: The small amplitude of the sodium leak currents recorded in 2 mM external calcium raises the question of whether inhibition of NALCN by dopamine would have a significant physiological effect on firing in the absence of GIRK activation (holding current at −70 mV; wild-type, −55.74 ± 4.29 pA, n = 39; NALCN KO, −19.69 ± 3.72 pA, n = 20; p < 0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Under control conditions, puff application of dopamine (300 µM, 1 s) resulted in a long duration pause in firing (47.88 ± 10.28 s, n = 8).
source: Under control conditions, we found that puff application of dopamine (300 µM, 1 s) resulted in a long duration pause in firing (47.88 ± 10.28 s, n = 8) as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Puff application of dopamine using a high concentration (0.5 mM) of extracellular BaCl2 alone resulted in a 73.81 ± 10.47% reduction in the firing (n = 5).
source: We obtained similar results using a high concentration (0.5 mM) of extracellular BaCl2 alone which was shown to completely block GIRK channels (Sodickson and Bean, 1996). Under these conditions, puff application of dopamine resulted in a 73.81 ± 10.47% reduction in the firing (n = 5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 0.5 mM extracellular BaCl2 alone completely blocks GIRK channels.
source: We obtained similar results using a high concentration (0.5 mM) of extracellular BaCl2 alone which was shown to completely block GIRK channels (Sodickson and Bean, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.
